passage: Through the thin wall of the flat in Toa Payoh, Wei could hear Ma and Ba arguing again, low and fast, about the rent. Her maths test was in her bag: 68 out of 100. They had argued last week too, the night her report book came home. So it was her. It had to be. She took out the test and redid every wrong question in neat pencil, then lined up all the shoes by the door. 'What are you doing?' her big sister Xin whispered. 'If I'm perfect, they'll stop.' Xin climbed onto the bunk beside her. 'They're arguing about the rent, Wei. Not you.' Next morning Xin told Ma, and Ma pulled Wei onto her lap before school. 'Grown-up worries. Not yours. Never yours.'

Monday: Sachin, nine, heard Mummy and Papa arguing in the kitchen, low and sharp, the same night his maths test came home with 12 out of 20. He lay in bed thinking: It's because of me. If I'd got 20, they wouldn't fight.

Wednesday: He made his bed without being asked, did his homework twice, and didn't laugh at cartoons in case the noise made things worse. When Papa sighed at the electricity bill, Sachin froze and quickly tidied the shoes.

Saturday: Mummy found him re-copying his test corrections at eleven at night. "Sachin, why are you still awake?"

"So you and Papa don't fight."

Tanuja sat on his bed. "Beta, listen. Papa and I argue about money and his long hours. Grown-up things. Never about you. It's not your job to fix it."

He wasn't sure he believed her. But he put the pencil down.

qa.a: Tanuja probably felt sad and a bit guilty that Sachin had been carrying their arguments. It likely made her want to protect him from that burden.

I'm Anand, and last winter my parents argued a lot at night in the kitchen, in low, sharp voices. I was sure it was because of me. The fights started the week I got 54 in maths. Once I heard Papa say "fees". So obviously it was my tuition, my marks, my fault.

So I became perfect. I made my bed before anyone asked. I did extra sums. If I'm perfect, I thought, they'll stop.

They didn't stop.

One night my mother, Vinita, found me awake, listening. She sat on my bed and I told her everything. She held my hand. "Beta, our arguments are about grown-up things, Papa's job, Nani's house. Not you. Never your marks. You don't have to be perfect to fix us."

The next day Papa said the same. I still did some extra sums. But I slept better.

qa.q: What did Anand score in maths?
qa.a: Anand scored 54 in maths.

qa.q: Why was Anand sure the arguments were his fault?
qa.a: Anand felt anxious and guilty, and the timing of his maths mark and the word "fees" seemed like proof that he caused the tension.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Anand, listened, and said clearly that the arguments were about grown-up things, not him, and that he didn't have to be perfect.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt finding Anand awake?
qa.a: Vinita was probably sad and concerned to learn he had been carrying the blame, and quick to reassure him.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4C, 2 December.

Vaibhav's homework has been too perfect lately. Today he burst into tears when he got one sum wrong. At lunch he told me quietly, "If I get everything right, Mummy and Papa won't fight. They fight because I'm bad at maths."

He said he hears them argue at night about money and "the shop". He said they are kind to him, and nothing suggested anyone is being hurt.

I told him grown-ups argue about grown-up worries, not because of children's marks, and that one wrong sum is completely normal.
This afternoon I shared this with our school counsellor, and we called his mother together. She was upset to hear it and said she and his father will both tell him tonight that it isn't about him. The counsellor will check in with Vaibhav on Monday.

Nitin
